open_obligations: Check that the training reward in the programming setup counts as a learned reward model in Leike et al.'s sense.
Check the oracle-reward control to confirm the effect comes from reward-model imperfection.
Check whether evaluators were time-limited, which may amplify the effect.
out.other_title: Reward gaming as possibly the greatest weakness of reward modeling
out.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether reward gaming can be overcome in practice. Wen et al. report RLHF raises human approval by +6.0% to +14.3% across three setups while barely raising correctness, which the authors read as RLHF making the model appear more convincing to humans without improving performance on the intended task; the three setups are QA under a general training reward, QA under a task-specific training reward, and programming.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether optimising a learned reward model improves the proxy and human approval without improving the true objective, for RLHF on QA and programming

text: The paper reports that across all three setups RLHF substantially increases human approval (+9.4% on QA with the general reward, +6.0% on QA with the task-specific reward, +14.3% on programming) but barely increases correctness, which the authors interpret as RLHF increasing U-Sophistry.
title: RLHF raises human approval (+6.0 to +14.3%) without improving correctness
